title: Baker McKenzie AI: Strategic Positioning in Legal AI
author: Dany Kitishian

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source shares the cluster’s view that AI requires service and business-model redesign rather than mere tool adoption. However, it redirects the buyer-centred proposition toward a provider-side thesis: proprietary development, data and client relationships will enable Baker McKenzie to create AI-native services and secure durable law-firm advantage. It does not substantively address whether legal departments will capture the gains or transmit them into pricing and staffing pressure.
qs: This strategy recognizes that the most profound value of AI will not come from performing old tasks faster, but from creating entirely new ways to solve client problems.

This integrated system will allow Baker McKenzie not only to lead in the application of AI but to define the future of AI-native legal services, moving beyond incremental efficiency gains to create entirely new sources of client value and solidifying its dominance in the global legal market for the decade to come.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports AI augmentation and efficiency in legal work, but it does not address direct-to-consumer access, users’ verification capacity, remedies, inequality, or the downward transfer of risk. Its adoption figures and market forecasts therefore do not establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: The focus has shifted from automating low-value tasks to augmenting high-value legal work.

Today’s AI tools are capable of sophisticated legal research, in-depth contract analysis, drafting initial legal memoranda, and even performing predictive analysis to forecast case outcomes.1 This shift is reflected in market sentiment and adoption rates.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI requires redesigning legal-service delivery rather than merely improving task efficiency. It materially extends that thesis by arguing that a law firm can develop AI-native, potentially productized services and defend them through proprietary global work product, internal R&D and technology-client co-development. Its claims of durable leadership and reduced bias remain predictions rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: This internal R&D engine is not just focused on improving internal efficiency but on creating novel, high-value, and potentially productized legal services, fundamentally altering the firm’s business model.

The convergence of these four pillars—strategic foresight, in-house creation, a proprietary data moat, and a client-driven innovation flywheel—creates a strategic advantage that is more than the sum of its parts.

st.t: Competitive strategy: Build-versus-buy becomes a portfolio
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s portfolio framing and materially develops it through Baker McKenzie’s combined use of external tools, proprietary platforms, partnerships and equity-backed ventures. It also locates differentiation in integrated data, expertise and delivery rather than model access alone, although its forecast of decade-long dominance is more confident than the cluster’s evidence warrants.
qs: This is a sensible approach for gaining immediate capabilities, but it again underscores the distinctiveness of Baker McKenzie’s dual strategy of both adopting best-in-class external tools and simultaneously building its own proprietary platforms.

The convergence of these four pillars—strategic foresight, in-house creation, a proprietary data moat, and a client-driven innovation flywheel—creates a strategic advantage that is more than the sum of its parts.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI can reshape legal-service business models rather than merely improve task efficiency. It materially extends the adaptation side by proposing an incumbent-firm strategy based on internal R&D, productized services, proprietary data and client co-development. However, its claims are largely forward-looking and do not directly evidence the cluster’s specific concerns about junior leverage, apprenticeship, employment or pricing.
qs: This internal R&D engine is not just focused on improving internal efficiency but on creating novel, high-value, and potentially productized legal services, fundamentally altering the firm’s business model.
This is not an incremental change but a fundamental paradigm shift in the creation, delivery, and valuation of legal services.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source accepts that AI adoption is a business-model and service-design challenge rather than merely a productivity exercise. It materially extends the cluster through a Baker McKenzie case study: combining external tools with proprietary development, multidisciplinary workflows, productised services and institutional data to pursue scalable delivery and differentiation. Its claims of a widening data moat, superior margins and decade-long dominance remain strategic projections rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: The tools developed by BakerML, however, are designed to handle “high volume requests” and deliver consistent, high-quality outputs with significantly reduced direct human input.16 This model breaks the traditional scaling limitation of law firms.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts AI as an operating-model and competitive transformation rather than a stand-alone productivity tool, then materially extends the cluster through a concrete incumbent-firm strategy: multidisciplinary in-house development, proprietary data, productised legal services, alternative pricing, governance and sustained organisational investment. Its claims of Baker McKenzie’s future dominance are forecasts rather than demonstrated market-wide outcomes.
qs: The tools developed by BakerML, however, are designed to handle “high volume requests” and deliver consistent, high-quality outputs with significantly reduced direct human input.16 This model breaks the traditional scaling limitation of law firms.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI value capture depends on integrated organisational and commercial redesign rather than isolated task efficiency. It materially develops that proposition through Baker McKenzie’s proposed combination of proprietary development, multidisciplinary capability, global data, productisation and new pricing models, while presenting competitive leadership and profitability as forecasts rather than demonstrated returns.
qs: This is not an incremental change but a fundamental paradigm shift in the creation, delivery, and valuation of legal services.
This represents a strategic shift from being a pure professional services provider towards a hybrid model that incorporates the characteristics of a technology company.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report accepts that legal-AI value depends on integrated organisational capabilities, redesigned service delivery, governance, testing and human verification rather than tool procurement alone. It materially extends the cluster with Baker McKenzie firm-level examples of proprietary development and productised workflows, although its claims of scalable dominance and a widening competitive lead are predictions rather than demonstrated market outcomes.
qs: This potential dominance is not predicated on a single tool or technology but on a deeply integrated, multi-pillar strategy that creates a powerful and defensible competitive advantage.

st.t: Incumbent advantage: AI investment may reinforce market leaders
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that an established law firm can convert organisational capabilities and sustained AI investment into a defensible competitive advantage. It specifically identifies long-term, partner-led governance and proprietary in-house development as mechanisms, while presenting dominance as a forecast rather than a measured outcome.
qs: This potential dominance is not predicated on a single tool or technology but on a deeply integrated, multi-pillar strategy that creates a powerful and defensible competitive advantage.

This long-term vision has been institutionalized through its comprehensive ‘Reinvent’ innovation program and is championed by dedicated, partner-level leadership, ensuring deep strategic alignment and sustained investment.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of workflow reconfiguration rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, framing generative AI as augmenting higher-value legal work and improving internal workflows. It also recognizes ethical and business-model challenges, but gives little attention to verification, uneven task performance, user capability or apprenticeship risks, and its stronger competitive claims are predictions rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: The focus has shifted from automating low-value tasks to augmenting high-value legal work.

It is simultaneously improving internal workflows, building new client-facing products, shaping global policy, and leveraging its structural advantages in data and client relationships to create a compounding lead.

st.t: Product promotion: Multi-agent claims lack demonstrated benefit
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s assessment: it contains Klover product promotion rather than substantive evidence about Baker McKenzie’s legal-AI strategy. It presents claimed benefits for a multi-agent decision system and an ambitious news service without measured outcomes, comparative support or evidence of operational deployment.
qs: delivers enterprise-grade decision intelligence through AGD™—a human-centric, multi-agent AI system designed to power smarter, faster, and more ethical decision-making.

kp.k: Integrated AI strategy underpins a prediction of market dominance
kp.d: Kitishian argues that Baker McKenzie's early strategy, internal development capability, global proprietary data and technology-client relationships create a mutually reinforcing competitive advantage. Dominance over the coming decade is the report's strategic prediction, rather than a reported market outcome.
qs: This report argues that Baker McKenzie is uniquely positioned to dominate the Artificial Intelligence-driven era of the legal industry.

The convergence of these four pillars—strategic foresight, in-house creation, a proprietary data moat, and a client-driven innovation flywheel—creates a strategic advantage that is more than the sum of its parts.

kp.k: Generative AI shifts emphasis toward high-value legal work
kp.d: The report distinguishes a first wave of machine learning and natural language processing in the 2010s, focused on e-discovery and document review, from a generative-AI wave supporting research, contract analysis, initial memoranda and predictive analysis. It reports a 2024 Thomson Reuters finding that 77% of legal professionals expected high or transformational impact within five years.
qs: The focus has shifted from automating low-value tasks to augmenting high-value legal work.

A 2024 Thomson Reuters report found that 77% of legal professionals believe AI will have a high or transformational impact on their work within the next five years, a significant increase from previous surveys.

kp.k: Adoption statistics and market forecasts frame competitive urgency
kp.d: The author cites a legal-AI software market forecast of USD 1.55 billion in 2025 rising to USD 12.12 billion by 2033, with a 29.27% CAGR. The report also attributes to Clio a rise in daily AI use among legal professionals from 19% to 79% in one year, using these figures to argue that coherent AI strategies are becoming competitively necessary.
qs: The global legal AI software market is projected to expand dramatically, growing from an estimated USD 1.55 billion in 2025 to USD 12.12 billion by 2033, which represents a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 29.27%.
one 2024 report from Clio noted that the percentage of legal professionals using AI in their daily work skyrocketed from 19% to 79% in just one year.

kp.k: Proprietary creation is distinguished from commoditized software adoption
kp.d: The author's framework contrasts firms licensing broadly available tools with firms investing in proprietary capabilities and AI-native services. He argues that licensing yields accessible efficiency improvements but limited durable differentiation, whereas collaboration between lawyers, data scientists and engineers can create distinctive, potentially high-margin services. Baker McKenzie is characterized as both adopting external tools and building proprietary platforms.
qs: Because these tools are available to all, any efficiency gains are quickly commoditized across the industry.
These firms are making the significant investment to build proprietary AI capabilities and develop novel, AI-native legal services.
Baker McKenzie’s dual strategy of both adopting best-in-class external tools and simultaneously building its own proprietary platforms.

kp.k: Early strategy and partner leadership institutionalize innovation
kp.d: The report dates Baker McKenzie's first formal AI strategy to 2017 and describes Reinvent as the firm-wide framework integrating people, processes and technology. It identifies Chief Innovation Officer Ben Allgrove and machine-learning practice founder Danielle Benecke as senior leaders, arguing that partner-level authority sustains resources and aligns AI development with business objectives.
qs: Baker McKenzie authored its first formal AI strategy in 2017, a clear indication of a long-term vision that predates the widespread hype surrounding generative AI.

This program serves as the strategic umbrella under which all AI initiatives are developed and deployed, ensuring they are aligned with the firm’s core business objectives rather than existing as siloed IT projects.

kp.k: BakerML reportedly accelerates cross-border breach notification advice
kp.d: The report describes a BakerML tool developed with the cybersecurity practice to analyze breach details against a global regulatory database and guide notification obligations. It reports advisory turnaround falling from days to hours or minutes and cites the 2025 Legalweek Best Use of AI award as recognition of the application.
qs: The BakerML-developed solution, a generative AI-powered tool, automates this process, analyzing breach details against a global regulatory database to provide guidance on notification requirements.
This has dramatically reduced advisory timelines from days to mere hours or even minutes, enabling clients to make faster, more confident decisions in high-stakes crisis situations.

kp.k: Employment drafting tool reports internal substantive accuracy results
kp.d: A second case concerns a custom generative-AI employment tool handling high-volume advice requests across 45 countries using proprietary legal know-how. The report attributes 100% substantive legal accuracy to testing by Baker McKenzie's own lawyers, not independent evaluation, and describes customization to client style and formatting preferences.
qs: This tool was designed to handle high-volume client requests for employment-related legal advice across 45 different countries.
Rigorous testing conducted by Baker McKenzie’s own lawyers demonstrated 100% substantive legal accuracy.

Furthermore, the tool is sophisticated enough to be tuned to the distinct style and formatting preferences of a particular client, delivering a level of customization that generic AI models cannot achieve.

kp.k: Productized services could decouple growth from lawyer headcount
kp.d: Kitishian interprets BakerML applications as a move toward a hybrid professional-services and technology business. Scalable, repeatable solutions with less direct human input could expand cross-border work without proportional hiring and potentially improve margins; the report presents these as business-model implications rather than measured financial outcomes.
qs: The firm is not merely using AI to make its lawyers incrementally more efficient at billing hours; it is using AI to create scalable, repeatable, and potentially productized legal solutions.
It allows the firm to handle a greater volume of complex, cross-border work without a proportional increase in headcount, leading to greater scalability and potentially higher profit margins.

kp.k: Global legal data is framed as compounding competitive advantage
kp.d: The report cites over 70 offices in more than 40 countries and 75% of revenue from multi-jurisdictional clients. It argues that accumulated multilingual work product could support globally capable models and a cycle of improved models, additional high-value work and further data. It also argues that data diversity positions the firm to reduce bias; this is a strategic mechanism asserted by the author.
qs: The firm’s unparalleled global scale—operating in over 70 offices across more than 40 countries, with 75% of its revenue derived from multi-jurisdictional clients—is not simply a measure of its size but the foundation of its strategic data asset.
By leveraging a dataset that encompasses a wide range of legal traditions, cultures, and languages, Baker McKenzie is uniquely positioned to build fairer, more robust, and more reliable AI systems.
This work, in turn, generates more unique, high-quality, multi-jurisdictional data, which is then used to further train and improve the models.

kp.k: Technology clients supply demand and collaborative development opportunities
kp.d: The report states that the firm advises 92% of Fortune 500 technology companies and 90 of the 100 largest companies by market capitalization. It argues that sophisticated client needs drive innovation and cites collaboration with ADAPT, including Google, Meta and Microsoft, on patent-data analysis and diversity, equity and inclusion in patenting.
qs: The firm advises an elite roster of the world’s most technologically advanced companies, including 92% of the tech companies in the Fortune 500 and 90 of the 100 largest companies by market capitalization.
In this partnership, the BakerML team is using its AI capabilities to analyze patent data and develop solutions to improve diversity, equity, and inclusion in the patent process.

kp.k: External ventures extend monetization and innovation beyond the partnership
kp.d: The author describes Scorealytics as an AI legal-data analytics spin-off in which Baker McKenzie retains a 35% stake, with Sententio tracking global ESG litigation. He frames the venture as a SaaS monetization route permitting technology-talent equity incentives. WEF C4IR participation, a £100,000 UK fintech counsel fund and German legal-tech initiatives are presented as additional sources of policy insight, technology and talent.
qs: One of the most sophisticated strategic moves is the spin-off of Scorealytics, an AI-powered legal data analytics company in which Baker McKenzie retains a 35% equity stake.

This venture allows the firm to monetize its deep expertise in legal data in a scalable, software-as-a-service (SaaS) model, which operates outside the constraints of the traditional law firm partnership structure.

kp.k: Competitor comparison emphasizes differing publicly stated strategic priorities
kp.d: The author characterizes DLA Piper as governance- and advisory-oriented, Clifford Chance as focused on internal productivity and risk management, and Kirkland & Ellis as practice-led in transactional and litigation work. Clifford Chance's secured Azure OpenAI-based Assist tool, formal governance and over 400 identified use cases feature in the comparison. These are interpretations of public initiatives, with qualified language about competitors' apparent priorities.
qs: **DLA Piper** has positioned itself as a leader in AI governance, ethics, and policy.
**Clifford Chance** demonstrates a robust and mature strategy for internal AI adoption aimed at enhancing productivity and managing risk.

Its governance structure is highly formalized, with a central AI & Innovation Board and AI Steering Groups in every practice area that have collectively identified over 400 potential internal use cases.
However, it appears to be a decentralized, practice-led approach rather than a centralized, firm-wide strategy driven by a dedicated AI development unit like BakerML.

kp.k: Hourly billing can undermine incentives for AI efficiency
kp.d: The report argues that time-based revenue makes automation internally disincentivizing because faster completion can eliminate billable hours. It reports increasing client demands for flat fees and recommends that Baker McKenzie proactively champion value-based and subscription arrangements, educating partners and clients to assess delivered value rather than time.
qs: Every task that an AI tool automates is a potentially lost billable hour.
This creates an internal disincentive to adopt technologies that streamline work.
Rather than reacting to market pressure, Baker McKenzie should proactively use its AI-driven efficiencies to pioneer and champion value-based and subscription billing models for complex legal work.

kp.k: Confidentiality, hallucinations and regulatory variation require human oversight
kp.d: The author identifies privilege, confidentiality when using third-party platforms, algorithmic bias and hallucinations as professional risks, compounded by divergent jurisdictional regulation. Continued governance investment, rigorous testing and human-in-the-loop oversight are recommended conditions for responsible deployment, rather than reliance on autonomous outputs.
qs: Key concerns include maintaining attorney-client privilege and data confidentiality when using third-party AI platforms, mitigating the potential for algorithmic bias in AI-driven analysis, and managing the risk of AI “hallucinations”—the generation of plausible but factually incorrect information.

The firm must continue to invest heavily in robust governance frameworks, rigorous testing protocols, and “human-in-the-loop” oversight systems to maintain the highest standards of professional responsibility and protect both its clients and its own reputation.

kp.k: AI capability requires multidisciplinary talent and sustained investment
kp.d: The report anticipates demand for data scientists, machine-learning engineers, AI ethicists and product managers alongside lawyers, with competition extending to technology companies and startups. It identifies partnership-compatible careers and compensation, continuing infrastructure and data-curation spending, and protection of resources through economic cycles as challenges to sustained capability.
qs: The firm will need not only elite lawyers but also world-class data scientists, machine learning engineers, AI ethicists, and product managers.

Creating a culture, career path, and compensation structure that can attract and retain this highly sought-after technical talent within a traditional law firm partnership model is a significant and ongoing challenge.
This long-term financial commitment must be sustained through fluctuating economic cycles and shifting partner priorities.

kp.k: Recommendations prioritize subscriptions, embedded specialists, training and acquisitions
kp.d: Kitishian recommends subscription products exploiting cross-border data, including compliance monitoring, supply-chain risk analysis and M&A checklists. He also proposes expanding BakerML into major practice groups, an AI Fellowship training associates in law and data science, and acquisitions of startups or specialist teams to accelerate capability development. These are proposed actions, not reported implementations.
qs: The firm should move aggressively to develop and market a suite of AI-native, subscription-based legal products.
The firm should double down on its investment in the BakerML team, expanding its mandate and embedding its specialists directly within every major global practice group.

Furthermore, launching a prestigious internal “AI Fellowship” program could help cultivate a new generation of hybrid lawyer-technologists, training top associates to be fluent in both law and data science, thereby building a sustainable pipeline of future innovation leaders.
The firm should leverage its financial strength to strategically acquire smaller legal tech startups or specialized AI teams.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kitishian argues that AI is moving legal services from routine-task automation to augmentation of high-value work and becoming a determinant of competitive position.
pts.d: The author distinguishes a first wave of machine learning and natural language processing used for discovery and document review from a generative-AI wave encompassing research, contract analysis, initial memorandum drafting and prediction of case outcomes. He predicts disproportionate market gains for firms that master this transformation and strategic obsolescence for those that fail to respond.

pts.k: Kitishian predicts a competitive divide between firms licensing generally available AI and firms creating proprietary AI-native services.
pts.d: In the author's 'Adopter versus Creator' framework, licensed tools deliver accessible efficiency improvements that become commoditized, whereas proprietary development can support distinctive, high-margin services. He places Baker McKenzie in the creator category through BakerML, while acknowledging that it also adopts external tools. His comparison portrays DLA Piper as emphasizing governance advice, Clifford Chance as emphasizing internal productivity and risk management, and Kirkland & Ellis as enhancing existing practices.

pts.k: Kitishian predicts Baker McKenzie's long-term market leadership from the interaction of early strategy, proprietary development, global legal data and technology-client relationships.
pts.d: The author argues that a formal AI strategy dating to 2017, the Reinvent program and BakerML combine with multinational work product and sophisticated clients to create a self-reinforcing competitive advantage. He claims diverse jurisdictional data enables more globally capable, less biased systems; better models attract additional work and data; and technology clients supply demanding use cases and co-development opportunities. Market dominance and widening performance advantages are the author's strategic predictions.

pts.k: Kitishian reports concrete service-delivery gains in cybersecurity response and multi-country employment advice.
pts.d: The cybersecurity example concerns an AI tool analyzing breach information against a global regulatory database to identify notification obligations, reportedly reducing advisory turnaround from days to hours or minutes. The employment example concerns draft advice across 45 countries, with client-specific style and formatting and reported 100% substantive legal accuracy in testing by the firm's own lawyers. These are presented as examples of new legal-service delivery capabilities, not merely generic office productivity.

pts.k: Kitishian predicts that scalable AI services can loosen the link between law-firm revenue growth, lawyer headcount and billable hours.
pts.d: The author interprets BakerML's applications as movement toward a hybrid professional-services and technology business, capable of processing more cross-border work without proportionate hiring and potentially earning higher margins. He presents Scorealytics, in which the firm reportedly retains a 35% stake, and its Sententio litigation-intelligence platform as a route to software-based monetization. Subscription products, expanded value-based billing, an AI fellowship and acquisitions are recommendations, rather than reported firm commitments.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Sector-wide transformation is supported with cited adoption surveys, professional expectations and a legal-AI software market forecast.
pts.d: Kitishian cites a 2024 Thomson Reuters report for the claim that 77% of legal professionals expect high or transformational impact within five years; Clio's 2024 reporting for AI use increasing from 19% to 79% in one year; and Straits Research for projected market growth from USD 1.55 billion in 2025 to USD 12.12 billion in 2033, at 29.27% CAGR. These are respectively reported expectations, reported adoption and a forecast, rather than measured future outcomes. The document does not reproduce their sampling or forecasting methods. General capability claims draw on legal-industry and vendor publications.

pts.k: The service-performance claims rely on firm-reported case studies, internal lawyer testing and award recognition.
pts.d: The cybersecurity example cites Baker McKenzie's March 2025 announcement of its Legalweek Best Use of AI award. The employment example cites the firm's May 2024 Client Management Innovation Award announcement. The author treats awards as external validation and reports internal legal-accuracy testing; the supplied article does not provide a test-set size, testing protocol, independent replication or quantitative comparison with competing systems. The reported accuracy pertains to that employment tool's testing, not AI legal advice generally.

pts.k: The dominance thesis is an interpretive synthesis of organizational facts, client statistics, partnerships and competitors' public initiatives.
pts.d: Kitishian cites firm materials for more than 70 offices in over 40 countries, 75% of revenue from multi-jurisdictional clients, relationships with 92% of Fortune 500 technology companies and 90 of the largest 100 companies by market capitalization. Reinvent, BakerML, ADAPT, World Economic Forum involvement and Scorealytics are offered as supporting cases. Competitor characterizations rely on publicly stated initiatives. The data-moat, reduced-bias and future market-capture claims are inferences from these inputs; the article presents no comparative model-performance results, realized margin gains or longitudinal market-share results for them.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article combines reported 2024–2025 capabilities with a roughly decade-long strategic forecast.
pts.d: Published July 28, 2025, the report traces routine-task AI to the 2010s and Baker McKenzie's formal strategy to 2017. It presents the cybersecurity and employment tools as existing capabilities, supported by 2025 and 2024 announcements respectively. Thomson Reuters' five-year expectation is anchored to its 2024 report, while the software-market projection runs from 2025 to 2033. The firm's predicted dominance is framed as extending through the decade to come, without a precise milestone or market-share threshold.

pts.k: Predicted competitive and financial benefits depend on changing billing incentives, maintaining human oversight, securing talent and sustaining investment.
pts.d: Kitishian identifies hourly billing as an adoption disincentive because automation can remove billable work. He conditions successful capture of efficiency gains on partner and client acceptance of value-oriented pricing. He also calls for confidentiality and privilege protection, bias mitigation, hallucination controls, rigorous testing and human-in-the-loop oversight. Continued investment in infrastructure, data curation and specialist staff must survive economic cycles and changing partner priorities. The argument therefore supports supervised service transformation, not unconditional reliance on autonomous legal advice.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are elite global law firms and multinational corporate clients, especially those needing high-volume cross-border advice.
pts.d: For Baker McKenzie, the predicted effects are differentiation, increased capacity, market capture and potentially higher margins. For firms relying on commonly available tools, the author predicts commoditized efficiency gains and weaker defensibility. Technology companies and multinational clients are both beneficiaries and co-development partners. Cybersecurity clients gain faster notification guidance; employment clients gain consistent, customizable multinational draft advice; proposed subscription customers would receive predictable-cost compliance and risk services. These are enterprise-service claims, not claims about closing the civil access-to-justice gap.

pts.k: Lawyers, partners and technical specialists face changed workflows, incentives and skill demands, rather than an explicit forecast of lawyer replacement.
pts.d: Lawyers are described as using AI to augment research, drafting and advice, with human oversight retained. Partners must reconcile efficiency with hourly revenue and fund long-term development. Data scientists, machine learning engineers, AI ethicists and product managers become strategically important hires, with law firms competing against technology companies for them. Kitishian recommends developing hybrid lawyer-technologists among associates. His scalability prediction implies less proportional hiring as work grows, but gives no numerical job-loss forecast or staffing-shape prediction.
